screens.title: Encapsulation and Access Specifiers in Unreal Engine
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn why encapsulation matters for building reliable game systems and how Unreal Engine's reflection macros layer editor and Blueprint access on top of C++ visibility. Encapsulation bundles data and the methods that act on it inside a class so internal state stays controlled and predictable. In practice this means storing core state, like a character's health or a door's open flag, behind private or protected members and offering public functions that enforce game rules when that state changes. Unreal's UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers then let you decide which values designers can tweak in the editor and which functions Blueprints can call. You'll see concrete examples, including a door actor that keeps its open state internal while exposing an editable open speed and Blueprint-callable open and close actions. We'll also cover common mistakes — for example, making everything public or using BlueprintReadWrite everywhere — and present a disciplined approach: minimal necessary exposure, prefer BlueprintReadOnly for state, and use BlueprintCallable for actions. By the end you'll be able to declare properties and functions that are both safe in C++ and useful to designers and scripters in the editor. How would you protect a key game state while still letting designers tune its values? We'll answer that step by step.

Why protecting state and exposing controlled interfaces makes gameplay code robust and designer-friendly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will develop concrete skills for protecting game state and creating designer-friendly classes. First, you'll understand the principle of encapsulation: how bundling data and methods inside a class prevents unintended state modification and keeps code modular. Second, you'll learn the meaning and practical use of the C++ access specifiers—public, protected, and private—so you can choose the right level of visibility for fields and helper functions. Third, you'll gain the ability to apply Unreal's UPROPERTY specifiers to control editor visibility and Blueprint read/write access, and you'll learn when to prefer read-only exposure. Finally, you'll practice exposing C++ functions to Blueprints using UFUNCTION specifiers such as BlueprintCallable and BlueprintPure. Each objective pairs a coding task with an editor or Blueprint example so you can both declare and test the effect in Unreal Editor. By the end you'll be able to decide which members stay internal, which are visible to designers, and which functions are safe to expose to Blueprints. We'll also point out common mistakes so you avoid over-exposing data and keep your project maintainable.

screens.title: Encapsulation: Definition, benefits, and analogy
screens.narratorSegment: Encapsulation is a core principle of object-oriented programming that bundles an object's data and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit, usually a class. The practical result is twofold: first, it prevents outside code from arbitrarily changing internal state, and second, it defines a clear public interface that other systems can depend on. A useful analogy is a car: you interact with a steering wheel and pedals, not with internal gears or fuel injectors. That separation is powerful for games. For example, a player's health should be modified through functions like TakeDamage or Heal rather than letting any part of the code set health directly. Encapsulation improves modularity — you can rewrite internal mechanics without changing callers — and enforces invariants, such as clamping health values or applying invulnerability windows. A common misconception is that encapsulation makes code slower or less flexible. In practice, it makes large systems easier to reason about and reduces surprising side effects. A contrasting poor practice is scattering state across public fields and letting many systems mutate them directly; that pattern quickly becomes a debugging nightmare. To test your understanding ask: what invariants must be preserved by this object, and which members should be private to ensure those invariants? That question reveals what belongs behind the public interface and what should remain internal.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Encapsulation
Definition and benefits

Encapsulation bundles data and methods so internal state is only changed through the class's controlled interfaces. This protects invariants and reduces coupling between systems.

Protects state from unintended external modification.
Makes code modular: internal changes don't force external updates.
Simplifies reasoning: public interface documents intended uses.
Key Takeaway

Design public methods that enforce rules; keep raw state private or protected.

Analogy: a car

You control a car through a small set of inputs. The engine internals are not exposed. Similarly, expose only the methods designers and other systems need.

Concrete example
Player Health

Keep current health private. Provide public TakeDamage and Heal functions that clamp values and apply invulnerability frames.

Common mistake: making every field public for convenience. This increases coupling and debugging cost.
Check your understanding
  • Which state changes must be validated by code?
  • Which values may be read by the editor but should remain write-protected?

screens.title: C++ access specifiers: public, protected, private
screens.narratorSegment: C++ provides three primary access specifiers that shape class interfaces. Public members are accessible from any code that can see the class; they form the outward-facing A P I. Use public for methods and constants you expect other systems to call. Protected members are visible inside the class and to derived classes; they are useful when you design a base class that lets subclasses extend or tweak behavior but you still want to restrict external mutation. Private members are accessible only inside the class itself; this is the strictest control and is ideal for core state that must only be changed through verified methods. Consider a door actor: mark its open flag private so only the class can flip it, use protected for helper values you want subclasses to adjust, and put the OpenDoor and CloseDoor methods in public so triggers and other actors can invoke them. A common misconception is treating protected as 'public for friends' — remember, protected only allows derived classes access, not arbitrary external code. When designing game systems, ask which callers should ever change a value. If the answer isn't 'everyone', avoid public. Prefer the least permissive specifier that still allows necessary behavior. That habit keeps interfaces minimal and bugs easier to trace.

keyIdea.text: Prefer private for core state, protected for subclass extension, and public only for intentional APIs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Access Specifiers
Access specifiers compared

Decide who can read or modify class members. Choose the least permissive specifier that supports your design.

Public
External interface

Used for methods others should call. Use sparingly for fields.

Protected
Subclass access

Allow derived classes to modify internal behavior without exposing to all code.

Private
Internal only

Best for core state and internal helpers. Enforce access through methods.

Pro tip: start private and widen to protected or public only when you need subclassing or external calls.
Concrete example
Door actor pattern

private: bool bIsOpen; protected: float DoorOpenDuration; public: void OpenDoor();

Misconception: protected equals public. Contrast: protected only grants access to derived classes, not arbitrary modules.
Check

Ask who should ever change this value. If not external code, keep it private.

screens.title: UPROPERTY basics: editor visibility and Blueprint access
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal Engine's UPROPERTY macro gives you control over how a C++ member appears in the editor and to Blueprints. EditAnywhere makes the property editable in the Details panel of any instance — useful for designer-tunable settings such as an open speed. VisibleAnywhere shows the value but prevents editing, which is ideal for runtime diagnostics like an open flag. BlueprintReadWrite allows Blueprints to both read and write the value, while BlueprintReadOnly lets Blueprints read only. Combining these with C++ access specifiers gives you two layers of control: code-level visibility and editor/Blueprint exposure. For example, you might declare a private variable with VisibleAnywhere so designers can see runtime state but only C++ can change it. Or use EditAnywhere with BlueprintReadOnly so designers can set an initial value but Blueprint scripts can't overwrite runtime state directly. Category organizes properties in the Details panel for usability. A typical mistake is granting BlueprintWrite access to internal state that should only change through vetted functions. Always ask who should change a value and prefer read-only exposure when possible. This discipline prevents conflicting modifications and keeps designers empowered without sacrificing invariants.

keyIdea.text: UPROPERTY controls editor visibility and Blueprint access; pair it with C++ visibility for disciplined exposure.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › UPROPERTY Basics
Common UPROPERTY specifiers
  • EditAnywhere: allow editing in the Details panel for instances and defaults.
  • VisibleAnywhere: show the value but prevent editing.
  • BlueprintReadWrite: Blueprints can read and write the property.
  • BlueprintReadOnly: Blueprints can only read the property.
  • Category = "...": groups the property in the Details panel.
Design note: use VisibleAnywhere for diagnostic state and EditAnywhere for tunables; prefer BlueprintReadOnly when only reading is needed.
Key Takeaway

UPROPERTY specifiers make your C++ work well with designers. Match editor exposure to intended usage.

Concrete mapping
Private + VisibleAnywhere

Designers can view runtime state; only C++ can change it.

Private + EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly

Designers set initial values in the editor; Blueprints can read but not overwrite runtime state.

Misconception check

Don't assume UPROPERTY overrides C++ access. A private variable with EditAnywhere still prevents other C++ classes from writing to it — the editor exposure is separate from code-level access.

screens.title: AMyDoor.h — declaring encapsulated properties and functions
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact AMyDoor header that demonstrates how to combine C++ access and Unreal specifiers. In the example the class keeps its open flag private and marked VisibleAnywhere so designers can inspect it but not edit it. DoorOpenDuration is private but EditAnywhere so designers can tune the time it takes to open. Public methods are declared with BlueprintCallable so level Blueprints or other actors can trigger opening and closing. This pattern gives designers access to reasonable parameters while preventing uncontrolled modifications of runtime state. A common error is to mark runtime state BlueprintReadWrite; that allows Blueprints to change state directly and may bypass rules implemented in OpenDoor or CloseDoor. There is also a pure function IsDoorOpen marked BlueprintPure and BlueprintCallable so Blueprints can check the state without creating execution flow. When reading such a header, ask: which variables are runtime-only and which are tunables? Are functions that change state callable from Blueprints, and are pure getters separated accordingly? This separation makes debugging easier and keeps gameplay rules centralized. AMyDoor.h — declaring encapsulated properties and functions means private state for runtime, editanywhere for tunables, blueprintcallable for actions, and blueprintpure for pure getters.. In practical terms, read the header to see private state, editable settings, and blueprint-callable functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › AMyDoor.h Walkthrough
Header snippet
// MyDoor.h
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AMyDoor : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

private:
    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, Category = "Door State")
    bool bIsOpen; 

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, Category = "Door Settings")
    float DoorOpenDuration;

    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, Category = "Door State")
    float CurrentOpenAlpha;

    void UpdateDoorPosition(float DeltaTime);

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Door Actions")
    void OpenDoor();

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Door Actions")
    void CloseDoor();

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintPure, BlueprintCallable, Category = "Door State")
    bool IsDoorOpen() const;
};
Explanation
  • bIsOpen is private and VisibleAnywhere — visible to designers for diagnostics but only C++ changes it.
  • DoorOpenDuration is EditAnywhere so designers can tune timing in the Details panel.
  • OpenDoor/CloseDoor are BlueprintCallable so designers can wire them into level logic.
  • IsDoorOpen is pure: safe as a read-only check in Blueprints.
Misuse to avoid: making bIsOpen BlueprintReadWrite. That would let Blueprints directly flip the flag and bypass guard logic in OpenDoor/CloseDoor.
Key Takeaway

Combine C++ visibility and UPROPERTY to make safe, designer-friendly classes.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › AMyDoor.cpp Walkthrough
Implementation snippet
// MyDoor.cpp
#include "MyDoor.h"
#include "Engine/Engine.h"
#include "Kismet/KismetMathLibrary.h"

AMyDoor::AMyDoor()
{
    PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
    bIsOpen = false;
    DoorOpenDuration = 1.5f;
    CurrentOpenAlpha = 0.0f;
}

void AMyDoor::BeginPlay()
{
    Super::BeginPlay();
    if (GEngine) GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Yellow, TEXT("Door initialized."));
}

void AMyDoor::Tick(float DeltaTime)
{
    Super::Tick(DeltaTime);
    UpdateDoorPosition(DeltaTime);
}

void AMyDoor::UpdateDoorPosition(float DeltaTime)
{
    float TargetAlpha = bIsOpen ? 1.0f : 0.0f;
    CurrentOpenAlpha = FMath::FInterpTo(CurrentOpenAlpha, TargetAlpha, DeltaTime, 1.0f / DoorOpenDuration);
}

void AMyDoor::OpenDoor()
{
    if (!bIsOpen) { bIsOpen = true; }
}

void AMyDoor::CloseDoor()
{
    if (bIsOpen) { bIsOpen = false; }
}

bool AMyDoor::IsDoorOpen() const
{
    return bIsOpen;
}
What to notice
  • Constructor sets defaults so the actor behaves predictably in editor and during play.
  • Tick calls a single UpdateDoorPosition to keep animation logic centralized.
  • OpenDoor/CloseDoor flip state only through controlled methods.
Best practice: centralize state mutation so any rule, like clamping or triggering effects, always runs in one place.
Key Takeaway

Keep mutation and update logic together and expose only intended actions to external systems.

screens.title: UFUNCTION specifiers: Callable, Pure, and event types
screens.narratorSegment: UFUNCTION controls how functions appear to Blueprints and the reflection system. Use BlueprintCallable for functions that perform actions and have side effects; these nodes include execution pins so they fit into Blueprint flow. Use BlueprintPure for read-only functions that return a value and have no side effects; pure nodes have no execution pins and are expected to be const. BlueprintImplementableEvent is a declaration Blueprints implement; C++ provides no base logic unless you call a helper. BlueprintNativeEvent allows both a C++ implementation and optional Blueprint override. Choosing the right specifier is important for clarity and safety. For instance, OpenDoor is a side-effecting action — use BlueprintCallable. A getter like IsDoorOpen should be BlueprintPure to indicate it won't change state and can be evaluated inline. A frequent misconception is using BlueprintPure for functions that read state but may implicitly change it; that breaks the contract of pure nodes. Also, exposing everything as BlueprintCallable increases coupling and can let designers invoke internal transitions at inappropriate times. Design your function exposure so Blueprints can drive behavior through well-defined actions while internal state changes remain controlled. Consider whether a function should be an event implemented by Blueprints or a callable action provided by C++; the difference changes where logic lives and who owns the rules.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › UFUNCTION Specifiers
Common UFUNCTION types
  • BlueprintCallable: exposes side-effecting actions as execution nodes.
  • BlueprintPure: exposes const read-only functions as value nodes without execution pins.
  • BlueprintImplementableEvent: declare a function Blueprints implement.
  • BlueprintNativeEvent: allow C++ default logic with optional Blueprint override.
Design tip: prefer BlueprintPure for simple getters and never mark a mutating function as pure.
Key Takeaway

Expose functions according to whether they modify state or merely report it; this improves Blueprint clarity and correctness.

Examples
Action

UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable) void OpenDoor();

Getter

UFUNCTION(BlueprintPure, BlueprintCallable) bool IsDoorOpen() const;

Misconception

Do not mark mutating functions as pure. Pure nodes are expected to be side-effect free and const.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes weaken encapsulation in game code. The first is making everything public or using BlueprintReadWrite everywhere. That convenience allows any system to mutate state and hides who is responsible for changes. The second is giving both code-level and editor-level write access to the same variable, which can create conflicts when C++ and Blueprints both attempt to modify a value. The third mistake is using BlueprintPure for functions that do more than return a value; that violates the pure contract and can confuse Blueprint authors. How to avoid these pitfalls? Follow a small checklist: keep core runtime state private, expose tunables with EditAnywhere but prefer BlueprintReadOnly, make mutating behaviors callable via BlueprintCallable functions, and centralize mutation logic in C++ so events and side effects run predictably. When you detect a bug, ask which systems are allowed to change this value and reduce exposure until only the correct owners remain. Discipline in access control leads to more maintainable gameplay code and faster iteration during level design and testing. Common mistakes and how to avoid them means restrict write access to a small set of owners and expose read-only editor visibility when possible.. In practical terms, over-exposure, blueprintwrite risks, and debugging complexity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Frequent issues

  • Mismatching C++ access and UPROPERTY exposure and assuming one overrides the other.
  • Using BlueprintPure for functions that implicitly change state or depend on side effects.
If debugging is hard, reduce who can write state. Often a single change in access specifiers reveals the owner and prevents accidental writes.
Key Takeaway

Limit writable access and centralize mutation so state changes are traceable and correct.

Practical checklist
  1. Is this property a runtime state? Keep it private.
  2. Does a designer need to set an initial value? Use EditAnywhere + BlueprintReadOnly if Blueprints shouldn't write it.
  3. Should Blueprints initiate a behavior? Expose a BlueprintCallable function instead of making the property writable.

screens.title: Deciding exposures: a short decision checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When you encounter a new member, use a short decision checklist to choose its C++ access and UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION specifiers. Fourth, if a function is purely a calculation or getter, mark it BlueprintPure so Blueprints understand it's side-effect free. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn why encapsulation matters for building reliable game systems and how Unreal Engine's reflection macros layer editor and Blueprint access on top of C++ visibility. Encapsulation bundles data and the methods that act on it inside a class so internal state stays controlled and predictable. In practice this means storing core state, like a character's health or a door's open flag, behind private or protected members and offering public functions that enforce game rules when that state changes. Unreal's UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers then let you decide which values designers can tweak in the editor and which functions Blueprints can call. You'll see concrete examples, including a door actor that keeps its open state internal while exposing an editable open speed and Blueprint-callable open and close actions. We'll also cover common mistakes — for example, making everything public or using BlueprintReadWrite everywhere — and present a disciplined approach: minimal necessary exposure, prefer BlueprintReadOnly for state, and use BlueprintCallable for actions. By the end you'll be able to declare properties and functions that are both safe in C++ and useful to designers and scripters in the editor. How would you protect a key game state while still letting designers tune its values? We'll answer that step by step.

In this lesson you will develop concrete skills for protecting game state and creating designer-friendly classes. First, you'll understand the principle of encapsulation: how bundling data and methods inside a class prevents unintended state modification and keeps code modular. Second, you'll learn the meaning and practical use of the C++ access specifiers—public, protected, and private—so you can choose the right level of visibility for fields and helper functions. Third, you'll gain the ability to apply Unreal's UPROPERTY specifiers to control editor visibility and Blueprint read/write access, and you'll learn when to prefer read-only exposure. Finally, you'll practice exposing C++ functions to Blueprints using UFUNCTION specifiers such as BlueprintCallable and BlueprintPure. Each objective pairs a coding task with an editor or Blueprint example so you can both declare and test the effect in Unreal Editor. By the end you'll be able to decide which members stay internal, which are visible to designers, and which functions are safe to expose to Blueprints. We'll also point out common mistakes so you avoid over-exposing data and keep your project maintainable.

This second set of objectives focuses on practice and error avoidance. You will create and test an AMyDoor actor that demonstrates encapsulation, learn to implement predictable door state transitions using C++ methods and Tick updates, and practice exposing properties and functions correctly so designers can tweak behavior without breaking invariants. You will also identify and fix common mistakes, such as making everything public or allowing Blueprints to write to state that should only change via C++ logic. Finally, you'll be able to choose the right specifiers for a given requirement: for example, giving designers an initial value via the editor but preventing Blueprints from directly modifying runtime state. Each objective is paired with a short hands-on step or decision checklist so you can validate the learning in the editor and in Blueprint graphs. By completing these objectives you'll be able to implement safe actor classes that are both engine-friendly and team-friendly.

Encapsulation is a core principle of object-oriented programming that bundles an object's data and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit, usually a class. The practical result is twofold: first, it prevents outside code from arbitrarily changing internal state, and second, it defines a clear public interface that other systems can depend on. A useful analogy is a car: you interact with a steering wheel and pedals, not with internal gears or fuel injectors. That separation is powerful for games. For example, a player's health should be modified through functions like TakeDamage or Heal rather than letting any part of the code set health directly. Encapsulation improves modularity — you can rewrite internal mechanics without changing callers — and enforces invariants, such as clamping health values or applying invulnerability windows. A common misconception is that encapsulation makes code slower or less flexible. In practice, it makes large systems easier to reason about and reduces surprising side effects. A contrasting poor practice is scattering state across public fields and letting many systems mutate them directly; that pattern quickly becomes a debugging nightmare. To test your understanding ask: what invariants must be preserved by this object, and which members should be private to ensure those invariants? That question reveals what belongs behind the public interface and what should remain internal.

C++ provides three primary access specifiers that shape class interfaces. Public members are accessible from any code that can see the class; they form the outward-facing A P I. Use public for methods and constants you expect other systems to call. Protected members are visible inside the class and to derived classes; they are useful when you design a base class that lets subclasses extend or tweak behavior but you still want to restrict external mutation. Private members are accessible only inside the class itself; this is the strictest control and is ideal for core state that must only be changed through verified methods. Consider a door actor: mark its open flag private so only the class can flip it, use protected for helper values you want subclasses to adjust, and put the OpenDoor and CloseDoor methods in public so triggers and other actors can invoke them. A common misconception is treating protected as 'public for friends' — remember, protected only allows derived classes access, not arbitrary external code. When designing game systems, ask which callers should ever change a value. If the answer isn't 'everyone', avoid public. Prefer the least permissive specifier that still allows necessary behavior. That habit keeps interfaces minimal and bugs easier to trace.

Unreal Engine's UPROPERTY macro gives you control over how a C++ member appears in the editor and to Blueprints. EditAnywhere makes the property editable in the Details panel of any instance — useful for designer-tunable settings such as an open speed. VisibleAnywhere shows the value but prevents editing, which is ideal for runtime diagnostics like an open flag. BlueprintReadWrite allows Blueprints to both read and write the value, while BlueprintReadOnly lets Blueprints read only. Combining these with C++ access specifiers gives you two layers of control: code-level visibility and editor/Blueprint exposure. For example, you might declare a private variable with VisibleAnywhere so designers can see runtime state but only C++ can change it. Or use EditAnywhere with BlueprintReadOnly so designers can set an initial value but Blueprint scripts can't overwrite runtime state directly. Category organizes properties in the Details panel for usability. A typical mistake is granting BlueprintWrite access to internal state that should only change through vetted functions. Always ask who should change a value and prefer read-only exposure when possible. This discipline prevents conflicting modifications and keeps designers empowered without sacrificing invariants.

UFUNCTION controls how functions appear to Blueprints and the reflection system. Use BlueprintCallable for functions that perform actions and have side effects; these nodes include execution pins so they fit into Blueprint flow. Use BlueprintPure for read-only functions that return a value and have no side effects; pure nodes have no execution pins and are expected to be const. BlueprintImplementableEvent is a declaration Blueprints implement; C++ provides no base logic unless you call a helper. BlueprintNativeEvent allows both a C++ implementation and optional Blueprint override. Choosing the right specifier is important for clarity and safety. For instance, OpenDoor is a side-effecting action — use BlueprintCallable. A getter like IsDoorOpen should be BlueprintPure to indicate it won't change state and can be evaluated inline. A frequent misconception is using BlueprintPure for functions that read state but may implicitly change it; that breaks the contract of pure nodes. Also, exposing everything as BlueprintCallable increases coupling and can let designers invoke internal transitions at inappropriate times. Design your function exposure so Blueprints can drive behavior through well-defined actions while internal state changes remain controlled. Consider whether a function should be an event implemented by Blueprints or a callable action provided by C++; the difference changes where logic lives and who owns the rules.

Several recurring mistakes weaken encapsulation in game code. The first is making everything public or using BlueprintReadWrite everywhere. That convenience allows any system to mutate state and hides who is responsible for changes. The second is giving both code-level and editor-level write access to the same variable, which can create conflicts when C++ and Blueprints both attempt to modify a value. The third mistake is using BlueprintPure for functions that do more than return a value; that violates the pure contract and can confuse Blueprint authors. How to avoid these pitfalls? Follow a small checklist: keep core runtime state private, expose tunables with EditAnywhere but prefer BlueprintReadOnly, make mutating behaviors callable via BlueprintCallable functions, and centralize mutation logic in C++ so events and side effects run predictably. When you detect a bug, ask which systems are allowed to change this value and reduce exposure until only the correct owners remain. Discipline in access control leads to more maintainable gameplay code and faster iteration during level design and testing. Let's summarize the most important terms from this chapter so you have a quick reference. Encapsulation is the idea of bundling data and methods so the internals are not modified by external code. Access specifiers — public, protected, and private — control who can read or write a member at the C++ level. UPROPERTY is the Unreal macro that exposes C++ members to the editor and Blueprints; specifiers like EditAnywhere and VisibleAnywhere determine editor editability and visibility. Keep these relationships in mind: C++ access controls code-level ownership; UPROPERTY controls editor and Blueprint exposure.
